terms.meaning: Cascading Style Sheets, the language that sets how a page looks: colours, fonts, spacing and motion.
a block of style rules. Here it sits inside the style tag of the page.
a named value, such as a colour, set once and reused across many rules.
a rule that applies only at certain screen widths, such as phone sizes.
a setting a visitor can turn on to ask websites to limit animation.
a free service that supplies the font files this page loads.
a drawing area in a web page where code paints shapes, used here for the 3D-style visuals.
GitHub's free hosting for websites built from a repository.

depends_on: Scripts later in this file (not in the packet)

sections.name: File setup (part 1)
sections.title: Page head and base styles
sections.what: Sets the page title, search and social preview text, the tab icon, and the font links. It also sets the base colours, fonts and text spacing, and the fade-in effect that reveals content as it scrolls into view.
sections.why: Likely reason: setting the base look in one place lets the rest of the styles reuse it.
sections.watch_out: The colour values here are reused across the page, and later style blocks replace them, so editing this block may have little visible effect.

sections.name: File setup (part 2)
sections.title: Top navigation and hero basics
sections.what: Styles the fixed top menu bar, which gains a solid background after scrolling, and the theme switch. It also sets up the top hero area with the name and the details list.
sections.why: Likely reason: the menu must stay readable over changing content, so it changes style once the visitor scrolls.
sections.watch_out: The solid background only appears when a script adds the solid class, and that script is not in the visible part.

sections.name: File setup (part 3)
sections.title: Hero identity card and filter chips
sections.what: Styles the name card in the hero, which opens and closes on click, with an animated plus sign. It also styles the small clickable chip buttons used for filtering.
sections.why: Likely reason: the card hides detail until a visitor asks for it, keeping the hero clean.
sections.watch_out: The card opens by adding the open class through a script that is not visible here. If that script fails, the card stays closed.

sections.name: File setup (part 4)
sections.title: Builds vault and project room pop-up
sections.what: Styles the builds area as a dark room grid where each project is a box that tilts and glows on hover, dims when filtered out, and has filter buttons. It also styles the pop-up window that opens for one project, with its 3D panels and video placeholders.
sections.why: Likely reason: the room layout presents each project as a physical space, which fits the memory-palace theme.
sections.watch_out: The hover and depth effects depend on the browser's 3D support, and the visual result cannot be checked from this code alone.

sections.name: File setup (part 5)
sections.title: Experience timeline and role cards
sections.what: Styles the experience section as a Gantt-style timeline, with bars for each period, a gold cursor for the selected point, and arrows to step between roles. It also styles the cards that describe each role.
sections.why: Likely reason: a timeline bar chart shows when each role happened and how the roles overlap.
sections.watch_out: The bar positions are set by a script and this file only draws them, so wrong numbers from that script would place bars in the wrong spots.

sections.name: File setup (part 6)
sections.title: Memory palace map styling
sections.what: Styles the interactive palace map: a dark drawing area, corner marks, a floating info panel for the selected item, a bottom toolbar and a route list. On phones it resizes the map and moves the panel to the bottom.
sections.why: Likely reason: the palace is a visual map of the owner's work, and its controls need a clear panel layout.
sections.watch_out: Line 281 is cut off in the packet, so the full rule that draws the grain texture is not visible here.

sections.name: File setup (part 7)
sections.title: Curiosity notes, about and contact layouts
sections.what: Styles the curiosity note blocks, which alternate between text and a visual on each side. It also lays out the about section in two columns, the contact list and the footer.
sections.why: Likely reason: the alternating layout gives each note a clear rhythm down the page.
sections.watch_out: Section padding set here is overridden later for small screens, so changing it may have no effect on phones.

sections.name: File setup (part 8)
sections.title: Pop-up dialogs and small-screen rules
sections.what: Styles the general pop-up dialog. Then sets rules for narrower screens: the menu links move behind a button, layouts stack into one column, and most animation is turned off for visitors who ask for reduced motion.
sections.why: Likely reason: the layouts need to fit phones, and some visitors need less motion for comfort.
sections.watch_out: The reduced-motion rule uses a wildcard, so it also stops any animation added elsewhere, including ones the owner may not expect.

sections.name: File setup (part 9)
sections.title: Clean theme overrides
sections.what: Redefines the colour and font values with a dark clean look: near-black background, Geist font, and a gold accent. It also restyles buttons, the menu, the hero, project tiles and notes to match. Because it comes later in the file, these values replace the earlier ones.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. The file layers several design passes, and the history of those passes is not visible.
sections.watch_out: Two later blocks redefine the same values again, so a change here may not appear. Search for the same selector before editing.

sections.name: File setup (part 10)
sections.title: Hero, about and contact refinements
sections.what: Restyles the about and contact text, the large contact headline and its gold highlight, and the contact links with a hover colour. It also moves the hero name card to the bottom left, adds a soft glow, and turns detail panels into floating boxes.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. These rules refine the look set earlier in the file.
sections.watch_out: The hero card and detail boxes use fixed positioning, so on unusual screen sizes they may overlap other content.

sections.name: File setup (part 11)
sections.title: Retro screen overlay and palace list rows
sections.what: Adds an old-monitor overlay across the whole page: faint scan lines, a slow flicker, film grain, darkened edges and a rolling highlight. It is turned off for reduced motion. It also styles the rows of the palace panel and the palace index grid.
sections.why: Likely reason: the retro overlay supports the terminal-style theme of the site.
sections.watch_out: The overlay sits above all content and lets clicks through, but it tints everything, so changing its strength alters the look of every section.

sections.name: File setup (part 12)
sections.title: Project wall, timeline progress and paper cards
sections.what: Styles the project wall, a floating list of project cards that slides in on the left, and the progress bar for the time-travel timeline. It also styles the photo, sector and paper cards and the globe canvas.
sections.why: Likely reason: the project wall gives a list view that sits alongside the visuals.
sections.watch_out: The project wall is hidden on small screens with an override that cannot be undone by other rules, so its content is not reachable on phones through this layer.

sections.name: File setup (part 13)
sections.title: Experience bento grid and nerd theme
sections.what: Styles the bento grid: mixed-size tiles that hold role details, stats, chips, a method list and photo strips. The grid reflows to six columns and then one column on smaller screens. Also sets the nerd theme, which switches the whole page to monospace type and a green-tinted palette when selected.
sections.why: Likely reason: the bento layout shows many kinds of experience in one dense view, and the nerd theme gives a second visual style.
sections.watch_out: Tiles use fixed column spans, so a new tile without a span will sit in an uneven place in the grid.

sections.name: File setup (part 14)
sections.title: Collapsible palace index and hero detail panel
sections.what: Styles the palace index as a collapsible block with a plus sign that rotates and a grid that slides open. It also places the hero detail panel at the bottom right and adds a blinking caret after the brand name.
sections.why: Likely reason: collapsing the index keeps the palace page short until a visitor wants the full list.
sections.watch_out: The slide open and closed depends on the open class added by a script that is not in this part, so without it the index stays closed.

sections.name: File setup (part 15)
sections.title: Styles for rooms, pointers and photos
sections.what: These style rules control how the small animated tiles in the AI builds vault look, how the floating note box looks when a knowledge row is opened, and how the photo strip and caption look inside the memory palace.
sections.why: Likely reason: the page keeps its styling inside the page itself, so each visual piece is styled next to the content it belongs to.
sections.watch_out: The knowledge note box switches to normal page flow below 900 pixels wide, so changing that breakpoint changes the phone layout.

sections.name: File setup (part 16)
sections.title: Styles for the build walkthrough screens
sections.what: These rules lay out the walkthrough of an AI build: the current screenshot sits in the centre of a corridor, the previous and next screenshots are angled on each side, and the information panel uses tabs. On narrow screens the corridor becomes a stacked layout.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. The angled side screens suggest a deliberate walk-through feel.
sections.watch_out: The corridor depends on 3D perspective settings, so small changes to the perspective or height values can make screenshots appear cut off.

sections.name: File setup (part 17)
sections.title: Loading 3D helpers and the top of the page
sections.what: Loads the last two 3D helper scripts used by the memory palace, then builds the top of the page: the navigation bar with section links, the opening name card with tagline and role, and the two side lists of knowledge rows that sit beside the portrait.
sections.why: The opening area is the first thing a visitor sees, so it holds the name card and the main navigation together.
sections.watch_out: The navigation links point to section ids such as builds and experience. Renaming an id here or in the section tag breaks the link.

sections.name: File setup (part 18)
sections.title: AI builds vault and experience timeline
sections.what: Sets up the AI builds section, with a vault area and filter bar that the script fills with rooms, and the experience section, with a timeline, previous and next buttons, and an education line. Visitors see the rooms and can step through jobs here.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. The section is written as empty containers that the script fills, which keeps the content in one data block.
sections.watch_out: These containers are empty in the HTML. If the script stops working, the vault and timeline appear blank.

sections.name: File setup (part 19)
sections.title: Memory palace, curiosities and about
sections.what: Holds the memory palace introduction, its enter and list buttons, the palace canvas with its labels and tour controls, and a palace index. It then adds the curiosities section, which the script fills, and the about section with its quote and text blocks.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. The palace is a visual way to see career moments in place, and the other sections give context.
sections.watch_out: The enter and list buttons work only while the script can find the ids enter and listBtn. Changing those ids silently disables them.

sections.name: File setup (part 20)
sections.title: Contact, pop-ups and content start
sections.what: Adds the contact section with the footer and the two pop-up windows: one for the room viewer and one general pop-up. Then it opens the main content block that the owner edits, starting with name, tagline, role, and the knowledge map counts and first eight AI builds.
sections.why: The pop-ups are placed at the page end so they sit above everything else. The content block is kept in one place so the owner can edit text without touching layout.
sections.watch_out: Several builds still show the placeholder text Add the description for this build, and that text appears on the live site.

sections.name: File setup (part 21)
sections.title: Remaining builds and early career entries
sections.what: Finishes the list of AI builds and fun builds, then records the early career entries: the satellite work at Manipal, the Madcue venture, the Delbomblr role, the Tecnova role, and the first part of the Evalueserve role with its projects and tags.
sections.why: Each job holds its projects, highlights and industries in one structure, which the timeline and the pop-ups read.
sections.watch_out: Start and end years are decimals, such as 2025.45. The timeline bar positions come from these numbers, so a typo moves the bar on screen.

sections.name: File setup (part 22)
sections.title: Later career entries and curiosity list
sections.what: Finishes the career entries, covering the rest of Evalueserve, Aranca with its many projects and tools, and the current Bain role. It then lists industries, extra builds and research topics for the palace, and begins the curiosity entries.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. Lists here are used by the palace and the knowledge map, so they are kept as plain data.
sections.watch_out: The Bain role ends at a fixed year number, not today, so the timeline will not extend on its own even though the text says Present.

sections.name: File setup (part 23)
sections.title: Remaining content and small helper tools
sections.what: Finishes the curiosity entries, the open question, the about text, the about table and the links. It then sets up small helper functions for finding page parts, escaping text, padding numbers and sizing canvases. It also fills the knowledge rows on the hero and starts the knowledge row handler.
sections.why: Helpers are kept in one place so every part of the page uses the same way to find elements and to protect text.
sections.watch_out: Content from the data block is placed into the page through the escaping helper. New text that skips this path could be read as markup, so keep using the helper when adding content.

sections.name: File setup (part 24)
sections.title: Knowledge note box and portrait outline
sections.what: When a visitor clicks a knowledge row, a note box opens beside the panel. Its items load from a separate data file. This section also starts the 3D portrait by reading the photo and finding the outline of the figure, using a fill from the edges and a largest-shape check.
sections.why: The note box loads its data separately so the notes can grow without changing this page. The portrait needs the outline to decide where dots should appear.
sections.watch_out: If home-data.json is missing or fails to load, the note box stays on the text Loading the map and never shows its items.

sections.name: File setup (part 25)
sections.title: Building the particle portrait
sections.what: Turns the photo into a cloud of glowing dots arranged to look like a head. It uses a hand-drawn outline so the face is not lost against a light background. It also places depth, adds background stars and prepares the dot appearance settings.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code, but the comments say the simple outline method would remove the face because the skin is close in tone to the wall, which explains the hand-drawn outline.
sections.watch_out: The hand-drawn outline is tied to the size of media/portrait/hero-particles.jpg. Replacing the photo means redrawing the outline or the face will not match the dots.

sections.name: File setup (part 26)
sections.title: Head motion, cursor reaction and connector lines
sections.what: Finishes the dot display so the particles scatter when the cursor moves and settle back afterwards. It rotates the head to follow the pointer and draws curved lines from the head to each knowledge row on wide screens. It also handles resizing and the toggle for the identity card.
sections.why: The head responds to the pointer to make the hero feel alive, and the lines link each knowledge row to the part of the head it belongs to.
sections.watch_out: The connector lines are skipped when the panels are not placed to the side, so on phones they disappear by design.

sections.name: File setup (part 27)
sections.title: Build room, screens and walkthrough controls
sections.what: Builds the filter buttons and the room tiles in the AI builds vault, and an archive pop-up listing every build. When a room is clicked, it opens the build room, loads that build's screenshots, and lets the visitor move between screens by buttons, thumbnails, arrow keys, or an automatic walkthrough that advances about every 4.2 seconds.
sections.why: The rooms are made from the data block so the vault stays in step with the list of builds.
sections.watch_out: Each room finds its build data by matching the name in home-data.json. If the name differs, the room shows the message that no screens exist yet.

sections.name: File setup (part 28)
sections.title: Build room tabs and animated vault rooms
sections.what: Fills the Demo, Stack and Run tabs of a build room. The demo tab shows a recorded video, the stack tab loads a layer diagram from the build's folder, and the run tab shows instructions. It then animates each vault room with frames that draw themselves and show the screenshots when a visitor hovers.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. The drawn frames give each vault room a sense of building and make hovering feel responsive.
sections.watch_out: The stack tab reads media/projects followed by the build's slug. A missing file shows the text Stack graph coming soon, which can hide a wrong folder name.

sections.name: File setup (part 29)
sections.title: Starting the building-screens and time line
sections.what: Loads the screenshots for each room in the building view, up to four per room, and shows a count of the total. It then draws the experience timeline, which has year labels, tick marks, and one clickable bar per job. It also sets up the spinning dotted globe that shows arcs from the home base to each place worked.
sections.why: Likely reason: the page needs these pieces ready before the visitor scrolls to them, so they are set up once at load. Reason for the exact year range is not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: The year range and the place coordinates are typed in by hand, so a new job in a new place or a year outside 2013 to 2027 will be drawn in the wrong spot or cut off.

sections.name: File setup (part 30)
sections.title: Shared sketch drawing toolkit
sections.what: Provides one set of drawing helpers used by every hand-drawn graphic on the page. These draw wobbly double lines, sparkle dots along the lines, rings, dust, and paper grain. Two more functions use these helpers to draw a small technical sketch for each industry and a sketched photo frame.
sections.why: The code comment says the goal is one consistent 'palace style' across all graphics, so every drawing looks like it came from the same hand.
sections.watch_out: Each drawing uses a random number generator seeded from the name or number given. Changing the seed logic changes every sketch on the page at once, and the random sources are mixed, so results can vary between visits.

sections.name: File setup (part 31)
sections.title: Job panels, tiles and photo viewer
sections.what: Builds the detail panel for whichever job is selected. It shows a set of tiles for the role, the globe, highlights, projects, tools, industries, papers, methods, photos and links. Clicking a tile opens a popup with more detail, and clicking a photo opens it larger or plays its video. The previous and next buttons move between jobs.
sections.why: Reason for the tile layout is not stated in the code. The tiles are built from the same data sections, so each job uses the same design without repeated markup.
sections.watch_out: Some text is split on fixed separators such as a middle dot or a dash. If the wording in the data file changes and the separator disappears, the title and description in the tile will be wrong. Some lines in this section are cut off in the review copy, so exact details there are unclear.

sections.name: File setup (part 32)
sections.title: Palace list and 3D stage setup
sections.what: Fills the plain text list of the memory palace and wires its show and hide button. It also starts a function that sets up the 3D palace, which only runs when the 3D library loads. If the 3D library is missing or the browser cannot draw in 3D, the page falls back to the plain list.
sections.why: Likely reason: some visitors cannot run 3D graphics, so the list is kept as a readable fallback.
sections.watch_out: The 3D code depends on the global THREE library being loaded first. If the script tag for it fails, the palace quietly drops to the plain list with no error shown to the visitor.

sections.name: File setup (part 33)
sections.title: Drawing the stone monolith and dunes
sections.what: Draws the 3D monolith, a tall tapered building with a narrow slit entrance, oculus on the roof, side wings, a causeway with obelisks, tiny figures for scale, and a field of dunes. Every line is drawn with a slight random wobble and is also turned into a cloud of small dots that give it a sketched look.
sections.why: The drawing is written by hand from points rather than loaded from a model file, which keeps the page light. Reason the dimensions were chosen is not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: The layout depends on fixed numbers such as the monolith width and height and the causeway length. Changing one of them without the others can make the figures float or the slit sit inside a wall.

sections.name: File setup (part 34)
sections.title: Emblems and project cards in the hall
sections.what: Creates a glowing ring emblem for each job, with a short set of initials in the middle, placed in an alcove in the hall. The current job gets a gold ring and a larger emblem. It can also make a text card with a project description and a region, drawn on a canvas and placed in the hall.
sections.why: Likely reason: each job needs a distinct and recognisable symbol in the hall, and the shape pattern repeats through a fixed list.
sections.watch_out: Initials come from a hand-written lookup table and then from the first letters of the company name. A new company name not in the table will get initials that may be unclear or repeated.

sections.name: File setup (part 35)
sections.title: Photo moments lifted into 3D
sections.what: Takes each role's photos and turns them into 3D clouds of dots. It estimates a depth map from the picture itself, then plays a short sequence for each moment: the depth map, the photo, the lift into depth, and a slow turn. It builds clouds only when a visitor enters that room, and it cycles through the moments automatically.
sections.why: The code comment says the depth is estimated from the image itself, so no depth data needs to be stored. Reason for the four-stage timing is not stated, though the labels suggest a short story is being shown.
sections.watch_out: Depth is only a rough guess from brightness and edges, so odd photos can show strange shapes. Each photo is read pixel by pixel, so many large photos can slow the page while a room opens.

sections.name: File setup (part 36)
sections.title: Camera path, controls and tour
sections.what: Moves the camera from an outside view, through a door, and into each job's room. Visitors can drag to look around, click an emblem to enter, use arrow keys, or use the previous, next and auto-tour controls. The camera waits in a queue of points so it moves smoothly from one to the next.
sections.why: The door path makes the trip into the hall feel like walking in rather than jumping. Reason for the 6.5 second tour interval is not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: Keyboard arrows are captured whenever the palace is visible, even if the visitor is trying to scroll the page. The auto tour also stops only when the visitor clicks stop, drags, or uses a control.

sections.name: File setup (part 37)
sections.title: Resizing and the per-frame update
sections.what: Keeps the 3D view sized to its box, changes the field of view on narrow screens, and updates every frame. Each frame moves the camera, spins the emblems, fades the frames, drifts the dust, and reads the camera position for the small readout. It also switches the palace into a full-screen mode when entered.
sections.why: Each frame is redrawn so the animation runs smoothly. Reason the screen-width threshold is 700 is not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: The frame loop skips drawing when the palace is off screen, but some parts still update state. Leaving full-screen must also restore the page scroll, which is handled here, so changes to that flow can leave the page stuck without scrolling.

sections.name: File setup (part 38)
sections.title: Curiosity notes and their drawings
sections.what: Defines a small 3D point drawing for each curiosity note, such as the tanks, the console layers, the stumps and the ball track. It then builds each note card, adds a read-more popup for it, and animates its drawing only when the card is on screen. It also fills the list of open questions.
sections.why: Each note has its own drawing so the cards feel distinct. Reason for drawing only visible cards is likely to save speed, but this is not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: Notes without a matching shape fall back to the default shape named C03, so a new note with a new code will look like that default drawing. Some lines in the shape definitions are cut off in the review copy, so exact shapes are unclear.

sections.name: File setup (part 39)
sections.title: Scroll effects, theme and start-up
sections.what: Adds a short flicker line across the screen every five to nineteen seconds, unless the visitor prefers reduced motion. It also makes sections fade in as they scroll into view, highlights the matching menu link, changes the navigation bar style over dark sections, and starts the palace, the theme and the main animation loop once fonts are ready.
sections.why: Likely reason: the flicker adds an old-screen feel. The timing choice is not stated. The palace waits for fonts or 1.5 seconds so the layout is measured correctly.
sections.watch_out: The flicker and the start-up depend on the theme being saved in local storage. If that storage is blocked, the code falls back to the default theme silently, so a visitor may see a different look than expected.

summary: Styling for the personal home page. The visible part is only the design rules, not the page content.
purpose: Make the home page look as intended: colours, fonts, layout, motion, and how it adapts to phones and screens.
why: Likely reason: the styles sit in the same file as the page, so the whole page is one self-contained file. Not stated in the code.
how: The browser reads the head first, which sets the title, tab icon and font links. It then applies the style rules from top to bottom, so later rules with the same name win. The packet shows only lines 1 to 754 of 2087. Lines after that, which include the page content and any scripts, are not visible.
inputs: The browser loading the page, the Google Fonts service, and classes that scripts add to elements, such as open, solid and in. Those scripts are not in the visible part.
outputs: A styled page with a dark theme by default, an animated hero, project tiles, timelines, a memory-palace map, a bento grid of experience tiles, and a retro screen overlay.
risks: Heavy effects such as 3D transforms, canvas drawing and overlays can slow weaker phones. Several style blocks override each other, so edits can be missed or undone by a later rule. Line 281 is cut off in the packet.
debug: If an element looks wrong, search for its class name and find the last rule that sets it. If fonts look wrong, check the Google Fonts link near line 16. If content stays hidden, check whether the reveal class in and the script that adds it are present. If colours look reversed, check the data-theme setting. If motion is wrong, check the visitor's reduced-motion setting.
